sections.title: The second explanation
sections.narration: How many explanations do you consider before you pick one? John Dewey argues in How We Think that good thinkers rarely stop at the first. He describes a person who has a rival hypothesis, and says this rival hypothesis, or conditional principle of explanation, prevents him from dogmatically accepting the first suggestion. That is a powerful idea. A first explanation arrives quickly and feels right. A second one slows us down, and it is what turns a guess into an inquiry. Think of a time when your phone, car, or computer stopped working. The first cause you thought of may not have been the true one. A habit of asking what else might explain this can save time and mistakes. This is our second video on Dewey's book, and it follows a different thread from the first, which was about how thinking begins. This time we look at curiosity, suggestions, and the discipline of testing them. Dewey wrote in 1910 about education, so some of his examples are old, but the habit he describes is still very useful.

sections.title: When a question stays alive
sections.narration: Dewey cares about curiosity, and he describes the moment it becomes useful. He writes that when the question is not discharged by being asked of another, when the child continues to entertain it in his own mind and to be alert for whatever will help answer it, curiosity has become a positive intellectual force. The key words are continues and alert. Many people ask a question and drop it once they receive any reply. Dewey says real curiosity keeps the question open and watches for clues. Consider how a good detective or a good student behaves. They carry the question with them and notice what bears on it. You can practice the same thing. Pick one question this week, perhaps why a certain habit of yours persists, and keep it in mind for several days. Write down anything that seems relevant. This is not a method he tested with experiments. It is an educator's observation. It still describes something familiar, which is that questions grow when we keep them alive.

sections.title: Why curiosity fades
sections.narration: Dewey is realistic about how curiosity behaves over time. He writes that in a few people, intellectual curiosity is so insatiable that nothing will discourage it, but in most its edge is easily dulled and blunted. That is a sobering and probably familiar thought. Children ask endless questions, and adults often stop. Dewey's explanation is partly about school and partly about habit. When questions are answered with scorn or with a quick fact, the habit of asking weakens. Today we might add that constant distraction competes with curiosity as well. The encouraging side of his point is that curiosity can be protected. He wrote his book for teachers because he believed adults shape it, for good or ill. You can treat yourself the same way. When you ask a question, give it a fair hearing and do not dismiss it as a silly one. Notice when you feel the little spark of wanting to know, and spend two minutes following it. That small act keeps the edge from dulling.

sections.title: When a story feels true
sections.narration: Dewey distinguishes kinds of thinking. In one kind, thoughts simply flow. He writes that if the stream of suggestions is controlled simply by their emotional congruity, their fitting agreeably into a single picture or story, we have the second type. This is the kind of thought that feels satisfying without having been tested. Think of how a conspiracy theory or a favorite excuse hangs together. It fits, so it feels true. Dewey is not condemning imagination, which is useful for creativity and daydreaming. He is warning against mistaking a pleasing story for a conclusion. A practical test follows from his idea. When an explanation delights you, ask whether it delights you because it fits the facts or because it fits your preferences. A story can be internally neat and still be wrong. The remedy is not to distrust all stories, but to ask what evidence supports each part. Treat the feeling of a perfect fit as a reason to check, and not as a reason to stop.

sections.title: Doubt and confidence earned
sections.narration: Dewey gives an example of someone who thinks in a disciplined way. He describes a man who was skeptical of what, from long habit, seemed most certain, and credulous of what seemed impossible, and who went on thinking until he could produce evidence for both his confidence and his disbelief. The example refers to Columbus, and it shows two sides of good thinking. First, a willingness to doubt what everyone accepts. Second, a willingness to take seriously what seems impossible, and to keep working until evidence settles it. The important part is the ending. He did not rely on stubbornness. He kept thinking until he could support his view. That is a standard we can use. When you find yourself very confident or very doubtful, ask whether you could say why. Could you list the evidence for each side? If not, your confidence may be borrowed. Dewey's example also reminds us that new ideas can look absurd at first, and that is not a reason to dismiss them, nor to accept them without checking.

sections.title: Discipline of the habits of thought
sections.narration: What separates good beliefs from poor ones? Dewey gives his answer with care. He writes that only systematic regulation of the conditions under which observations are made and severe discipline of the habits of entertaining suggestions can secure a decision that one type of belief is vicious and the other sound. In simpler words, you need good conditions for observing and good habits for handling your ideas. A science experiment controls the conditions. A thoughtful person controls the habit of jumping to conclusions. You can build a small version of this discipline. When you have a theory about a coworker or a symptom, write down what you actually observed, and separate it from what you inferred. Then list one other possible explanation. Dewey's language sounds strict, and the standard is high, but you do not need to meet it perfectly. A little regulation of how you gather facts and weigh guesses already improves most decisions, and it costs only a few minutes of attention.

sections.title: A belief reached by a method
sections.narration: We have followed Dewey through six ideas: the rival hypothesis, living curiosity, fading curiosity, stories that feel true, earned confidence, and disciplined observation. A line from the book gathers them. Even if his conclusion had finally turned out wrong, he writes, it would have been a different sort of belief from those it antagonized, because it was reached by a different method. That is a deep point. The quality of a belief depends partly on how you arrived at it. Remember what this book is. It is a 1910 work on education, and later research has added a great deal about how people reason. Read the original chapters and judge for yourself. The useful ending is a precise question. Think of a belief you hold firmly. What method brought you to it, and what other explanation have you honestly tested against it? Write down one answer, and subscribe to MindLore for psychology read from the original texts.
